title: Pentatonic Scales
description: Five-note scales that turn up everywhere, from folk tunes to guitar solos. Play the major and minor versions.

steps.title: Five notes instead of seven
steps.description: 'Penta' means five. A pentatonic scale drops two notes from the usual seven, and the two it drops are the ones sitting a half step from a neighbor. With those gone, nothing rubs, so the notes sound good together in almost any order. That's why pentatonic melodies show up in blues, rock, pop, country and folk music all over the world.

steps.title: C major pentatonic
steps.description: Play C, D, E, G, A. It's C major with F and B left out, and without them the scale sounds open and sunny.
steps.hint: Any octave works. Skip F and B on the way up.

steps.title: A minor pentatonic
steps.description: Play A, C, D, E, G. This is the go-to scale for a lot of rock and blues solos, on guitar and keys alike.
steps.hint: Start on A and skip B and F.

steps.title: Same notes, different home
steps.description: Look closely: C major pentatonic and A minor pentatonic use exactly the same five notes. C-D-E-G-A and A-C-D-E-G. Scales that share notes like this are called relatives. What changes is the note that feels like home. Land on C and it sounds major; land on A and it sounds minor.

steps.title: G major pentatonic
steps.description: Now move it to G: G, A, B, D, E. It's the same pattern of steps as C major pentatonic, starting on G.
steps.hint: All white keys. You're skipping C and F#, the fourth and seventh notes of G major.

steps.title: How many?
steps.description: How many notes are in a pentatonic scale?
